The groups emphasize the connection between environmental issues and human rights, calling for accountability and the rejection of the Pax Silica initiative, which threatens indigenous rights.

MANILA, Philippines – Filipino climate justice and environmental advocates present at the UN Climate Change Conference (COP31) in Antalya, Turkey, are urging an independent probe into the mass arrests of people who joined the protests against the ASEAN Summit back in Manila.

“Whether at COP31 or the ASEAN Summit, the government cannot speak of a peoples-centered future while treating their voices as a security threat,” read the groups’ statement released Monday, November 16.
They demanded “an independent, transparent and immediate investigation into the arbitrary mass arrests and illegal detention.”
Climate justice activists underscored the link between the fight for the planet and for human rights and democratic freedoms.
“We stand in solidarity with the victims of this police brutality, their families, and the communities demanding accountability,” they said.

A key issue in the ASEAN protests is the Philippines’ participation in the United States’ initiative Pax Silica — a red flag for environmental groups for its components of building data centers and processing critical minerals.

The groups called on the government to “reject the Pax Silica initiative and all related projects affecting ancestral domains, respecting the right of affected indigenous peoples to free, prior, and informed consent.”
Some of the climate organizations listed as signatories in the statement have members or allies who were arrested in the protests in Manila.

The 49th ASEAN Summit, hosted by the Philippines, opened on Sunday, November 15. Hundreds who massed up for the protests in Metro Manila on Sunday were arrested. Nearly 300 people, delegates of Lakbayan ng Timog Katagalugan opposing the expected visit of US President Donald Trump, were arrested in Muntinlupa.
There were also arrests in Bulacan, Liwasang Bonifacio, Malate Church, and Welcome Rotonda in Quezon City, according to various local environmental and human rights groups.

“This is one of the largest mass arrests by the PNP (Philippine National Police) in recent years,” the International Coalition for Human Rights in the Philippines noted. The network has started a donation drive for legal funds to support those arrested.
Even before the opening of the ASEAN Summit, thousands of students had already walked out and marched on the streets.
Meanwhile, Bishop Gerry Alminaza, climate champion of the Catholic Bishops Conference of the Philippines, called on the government to “stop criminalizing the poor.”

“It is unconscionable that the poor are met with police violence when they should be met with justice, protection and action,” Alminaza, who was also in Turkey for the climate summit, said in a separate statement on Monday. – Rappler.com
